For the first part of this course we focused on working with data in R and RStudio,
including using `ggplot2` to explore and visualise relationships. More recently we
have looked at probability distributions, sampling variation and the central limit
theorem, which give us a way to think about uncertainty in estimates from data.

In this workshop we start bringing those ideas together. We will use plots to explore
relationships between vehicle characteristics and fuel use, then fit our first
regression models to describe those relationships numerically. Along the way we will interpret the fitted line, coefficients, $R^2$, predictions
and residuals. Then we ask how uncertain the fitted line is, and whether its
assumptions are believable.

[Waka Kotahi's vehicle-fleet data](https://www.nzta.govt.nz/resources/new-zealand-motor-vehicle-register-statistics/new-zealand-vehicle-fleet-open-data-sets)
provide a snapshot of vehicles recorded on the Motor Vehicle Register, while
[EECA's guide to vehicle energy-economy labels](https://www.eeca.govt.nz/regulations/vehicle-emissions-and-energy-economy-labelling-programme/about-the-vehicle-emissions-and-energy-economy-labelling-programme/)
explains the standard fuel-economy measure in litres per 100 km. The supplied
extract contains 467 unique vehicle specifications, prepared from Waka Kotahi's
vehicle-fleet data as at **31 July 2026** and containing model-year 2025 petrol
passenger cars and vans with complete measurements.
Download the supplied extract here: [2025 cars dataset](https://knowlton.co.nz/297101/labs/nz_vehicles_2025.csv).

## Today's question

How much can one vehicle specification tell us about fuel use?

## Learning objectives

By the end of this workshop you should be able to:

- recognise an approximately linear association from a scatterplot;
- fit and interpret a simple linear regression model;
- interpret the slope, intercept and $R^2$;
- calculate and interpret a fitted value;
- define and interpret a residual;
- interpret the standard error, 95% confidence interval and p-value for a slope;
- distinguish a confidence interval for an average from a prediction interval
  for one vehicle; and
- use residual plots to check the L-I-N-E assumptions and screen for
  influential observations.

## How to use this workbook

Work through the sections in order. Run the supplied demonstrations and look at
their output before moving on. In each **Your turn** section, write your own
code in the blank chunk, then answer the question in words. Hints appear when a
function or idea is first introduced; later tasks expect you to reuse it.
Open this file from the `labs` folder so the supplied data file can be found.

## 1. Explore engine size and power

**What to do:** Start by looking at the data before fitting a model. For each
scatterplot, describe the direction, strength and shape of the relationship and
look for anything unusual. Then calculate the correlation and ask whether a
straight line looks like a reasonable summary.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
library(broom)

vehicles <- read_csv("https://knowlton.co.nz/297101/labs/nz_vehicles_2025.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(vehicles)
```

Each row is one unique 2025 petrol vehicle specification. Fuel use is the
combined-cycle test value in litres per 100 km, so the plots describe
associations among specifications rather than causal effects or real-world
consumption.

### Demonstration: engine size

Let's start with the flexible smoother we learned earlier in the course to get a feel
for the relationship between engine size and fuel use. A reminder that this
lets us look at the *shape* of the relationship first and decide whether a linear
model is a reasonable summary.

```{r}
ggplot(vehicles, aes(engine_l, fuel_use_l_per_100km)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Engine size (litres)",
    y = "Combined fuel use (L/100 km)",
    title = "Do larger engines tend to use more fuel?"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

vehicles |>
  summarise(engine_correlation = cor(engine_l, fuel_use_l_per_100km))
```

Look at the scatterplot first. Describe the direction, shape and strength of
the relationship, and note anything unusual. Then use the correlation to
summarise its linear strength. Does that number support what you saw? Remember
that correlation has no units and is not a slope.

## 2. Fit simple linear models

**What to do:** Fit a simple linear regression model with fuel use as the
response and engine size as the explanatory variable. Identify the intercept and
slope, then add the fitted regression line to the scatterplot. Repeat the same
process using engine power.

You have now examined the shape of the relationship. We will fit a
straight-line model and compare it with the pattern you saw in the data.

A simple linear model describes the average response as a straight-line
function of one explanatory variable:

$$
\widehat{y} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x.
$$

```{r}
engine_model <- lm(
  fuel_use_l_per_100km ~ engine_l,
  data = vehicles
)

engine_model
```

```{r}
ggplot(vehicles, aes(engine_l, fuel_use_l_per_100km)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Engine size (litres)",
    y = "Combined fuel use (L/100 km)",
    title = "A straight-line model for engine size and fuel use"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

There are many possible straight lines we could draw through these data.
`lm()` uses least squares: it chooses the intercept and slope that minimise the
sum of the squared vertical distances between the observed values and the fitted
line. This is the same idea as minimising the mean squared error we looked at
previously.

What is `lm()` changing when it searches for the best-fitting line?

Compare the fitted line with the points. Does it capture the main pattern you
saw earlier? What variation remains around the fitted line?

From the printed model, identify the intercept and slope. What does the fitted
line represent for vehicles with the same engine size?

## 5. What is a residual?

For one vehicle, the residual is observed fuel use minus fitted fuel use:

$$
e_i = y_i-\hat{y}_i
$$

A positive residual means the observed fuel use was above the fitted value; a
negative residual means it was below.

**What to do:** Use `augment()` to compare the observed fuel use, fitted value
and residual for several vehicles. Check that

$$
\text{residual}=\text{observed}-\text{fitted}.
$$

Find one positive residual and one negative residual and explain what each means
in the context of fuel use.

**Hint:** In the augmented results, the observed response is
`fuel_use_l_per_100km`, the fitted value is `.fitted`, and the residual is
`.resid`.

```{r}
# Your code here
```

On the plot, the residual is the vertical distance from each observed value to
the fitted line. Before looking at the residual column, use the graph to decide
whether a point should have a positive or negative residual.

Use the plot to find one point above the fitted line and one below it. Predict

**Hint:** The residual is the observed value minus the fitted value.

## 6. How uncertain is the slope?

**What to do:** These estimates come from one set of vehicle specifications.
Use the coefficient table to read the standard error, 95% confidence interval
and p-value for the slope. State the null hypothesis being tested and keep
statistical evidence separate from practical importance and causality.

If we had a different, comparable set of vehicles, we would get a slightly
different fitted slope. The **standard error** estimates how much the slope
would vary across those samples. The t statistic is the estimate divided by its
standard error, and the p-value tests $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$, no linear relationship
in the population.

### Demonstration: the engine-size slope

```{r}
summary(engine_model)
tidy(engine_model, conf.int = TRUE)
```

Find the engine-size row. For this test, $H_0:\beta_{\mathrm{engine}}=0$ and
$H_A:\beta_{\mathrm{engine}}\ne0$. Does the 95% confidence interval include
zero, and does that agree with the p-value? Interpret the interval in
L/100 km per litre.

A p-value is calculated assuming the null and the model are true. It is not the
probability that the null is true, and a large p-value never proves the null.

## 7. The average vehicle or one vehicle?

**What to do:** Use `predict()` to calculate both intervals for a vehicle with a
2.0 L engine. Compare their widths and explain why they differ.

A **confidence interval** describes uncertainty about the *average* fuel use of
all 2.0 L vehicles. A **prediction interval** describes where *one new* 2.0 L
vehicle's fuel use might fall, so it also includes the vehicle-to-vehicle
variation around the line.

### Demonstration: confidence interval for the average

```{r}
new_vehicle <- tibble(engine_l = 2)

predict(engine_model, newdata = new_vehicle, interval = "confidence")
```

## 8. Check the L-I-N-E assumptions

**What to do:** Every standard error, p-value and interval above assumed L-I-N-E.
Work through the assumptions one at a time for the engine-size model. For each
one, say what pattern would be reassuring, what you actually see, and whether it
matters. Departures happen in degrees; they are not pass/fail rules.

### Demonstration: L and E, residuals against fitted values

```{r}
plot(engine_model, which = 1)
```

If the straight line is the right shape, the residuals scatter evenly around
zero with no curve. If the spread is constant, the vertical scatter stays about
the same width from left to right.

### Your turn: linearity and equal variance

Look at the red trend line and the width of the cloud. Is there a curve the line
has missed? Does the spread change as the fitted values increase? Then check
the spread again with the scale-location plot.

```{r}
plot(engine_model, which = 3)
```

### Demonstration: I, independence comes from the design

No plot of these residuals can show independence. Each row is a unique vehicle
specification, but several rows are variants of the same make and model, often
sharing an engine.

### Your turn: independence

Why might two variants of the same model have related residuals? What would you
want to know about how this dataset was built?

### Demonstration: N, the Q-Q plot

```{r}
plot(engine_model, which = 2)
```

If the residuals were normal, the points would follow the dashed line. Look at
the centre first, then the tails.

### Your turn: normality

Where do the residuals depart from the line? Are those departures in the
centre or in the tails, and are they on one side?

### Demonstration: influence

```{r}
plot(engine_model, which = 5)

augment(engine_model, data = vehicles) |>
  slice_max(.cooksd, n = 5) |>
  select(make, model, body_type, engine_l, fuel_use_l_per_100km, .cooksd)
```

Cook's distance measures how much the fitted line would move if that vehicle
were left out. A large value is a reason to check the record, not to delete it.

### Your turn: investigate influence

Which vehicles have the largest Cook's distances? Are they unusual in engine
size, in fuel use, or both? Would you remove any of them? Why or why not?
